thread.title: Will Bulls Or Bears Win As The S&P 500 Faces Key Test Of Support? | Investor's Business Daily

author: NANCY GONDO
title: Will Bulls Or Bears Win As The S&P 500 Faces Key Test Of Support? | Investor's Business Daily
text:
The stock market had a tough week during which the S&P 500 tested its 50-day moving average and the Nasdaq composite tumbled below its own 50-day line.
X That means the S&P 500 faces a crucial test. Will the broad benchmark index find support and rebound off the line? Or will it follow the Nasdaq's footsteps and slice through the 50-day?
Exchange traded funds tracking the S&P 500 are tracing a similar pattern. If they bounce off the line, that could mark an opportunity to buy shares. If not, it might be prudent to wait until another chance emerges, such as a powerful advance to retake the line or a breakout from a base.
With that in mind, let's take a look at some of the biggest ETFs that track the S&P 500.
The Big Trio SPDR S&P 500 ( SPY ): This is the granddaddy of all ETFs. State Street launched the fund — the first U.S. ETF — in 1993. Today it's the biggest fund in the world, with a whopping $279.3 billion in assets. It tracks the market-weighted S&P 500 index and carries a 0.09% expense ratio.
The top five holdings — Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Berkshire Hathaway ( BRKB ) and JPMorgan ( JPM ) — account for 14% of total assets.
SPY's year-to-date return through Thursday was 9.9%, slightly behind the benchmark index's 10.1% gain. The ETF's average annual returns over the past three, five and 10 years, respectively, were 16.4%, 13.6% and 12.4%. Those are also close to the S&P 500's 16.5%, 13.7% and 12.6% gains for the same periods.
IShares Core S&P 500 ( IVV ): The $162.5 billion fund, which launched in May 2000, charges 4 basis points. Similar to SPY, the BlackRock ETF's same top five holdings make up 14% of the fund's portfolio. IVV is up 10% year to date, according to Morningstar Inc. Its average annual returns for the past three, five and 10 years of 16.5%, 13.7% and 12.5% are virtually in line with the S&P 500.
Vanguard S&P 500 ( VOO ): This is the youngest of the trio, with an inception date of Sept. 7, 2010. Like IVV, this $104.5 billion Vanguard fund bears a 0.04% expense ratio. The top five holdings as of Aug. 31 were Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook ( FB ) and JPMorgan. They represented nearly 15% of total assets. VOO was up 9.9% for this year through Thursday's close. Its three- and five-year average annual returns were 16.5% and 13.7%.
